About

EvaluativeCase study 01 · Usability testing

100% task success, and still a shadow system in Excel

A usability study of the Award Request List in SAGE, the University of Washington's grant-management system, done with the SAGE product team in UW's Office of Research.

My role
UX researcher on a team of 4: study design, moderation, analysis, readout
Timeline
Jan to Feb 2026
Methods
Heuristic evaluation, moderated usability testing, think-aloud, SUS
Stakeholder
SAGE product and engineering team, UW Office of Research

The problem

Experienced grant managers kept their own spreadsheets to track requests SAGE was built to track. The team had complaints but no evidence of which problems cost the most.

What we did

A heuristic evaluation to find likely issues cheaply, then 5 moderated sessions with expert users across four schools, scored by a four-factor severity rubric.

What changed

The product team triaged our recommendations into its backlog with tickets and priorities, and later reached the same root diagnosis in its own independent analysis.

ContextQuestionsApproachFindingsRecommendationsImpactReflection

Stage 1 · Planning · Context

The list grant managers use to run their day

Campus grant administrators use SAGE's Award Request List to track Award Setup Requests and Modification Requests, the two workflows that move every research award through review. Earlier feedback had flagged search, status tracking and visibility, but feedback alone couldn't tell the team which problems mattered most, or why experienced people were still building workarounds.

The surprising part came early. All 5 participants completed every task, and 4 of 5 made critical errors along the way. Task success was measuring how good experts had become at routing around the system. That gap became the core argument of the study.

Stage 1 · Planning · Research questions

Breaking "is it usable?" into five testable questions

RQ1 · Search & filterHow well can users find a specific request with the current search and filters?
RQ2 · StatusHow clearly does the system communicate status and the next required action?
RQ3 · PrioritizationHow do users plan their daily workload from the list?
RQ4 · WorkaroundsWhat do users do outside SAGE to compensate for its limits?
RQ5 · OwnershipHow do users tell their own action items from items waiting on someone else?

Stages 1–2 · Planning and research · Approach

Spend expert hours only on what needs real users

Participants were scarce: a small, credentialed user base with full calendars. So we used a cheap method first to decide what the expensive method should test.

  1. Heuristic evaluationScored the interface against Nielsen's 10 heuristics with severity ratings.
  2. Test planTurned the top issues into 3 realistic task scenarios.
  3. RecruitTargeted outreach across four schools; weekly users with 3+ months on SAGE.
  4. 5 sessionsRemote, moderated, ~55 min each, think-aloud plus SUS.
  5. Severity scoringFrequency, impact, persistence and frustration for each issue.
  6. ReadoutRecommendations mapped to the team that owns each fix.
Participants
N = 5 expert users, 1 to 20+ years on the job: Medicine, Computer Science, Education, Engineering
Session
5 min context interview, 30 to 40 min tasks, 10 min post-study questionnaire
Measures
Task completion, error counts (search, navigation, selection), post-task 1 to 5 ratings, SUS
SUS result
add mean SUS score

Stage 3 · Synthesis · Findings

Three high-severity issues pushed people out of the system

Before the problems: status labels were rated clear (4 of 5 gave 4 or 5 out of 5), and all 5 went straight to Comments & History for context. We weren't asking the team to rebuild SAGE, only to close specific gaps.

High severity

Filters disappear after every click into a record

Opening a request and coming back wiped every applied filter, so each look at a detail meant rebuilding the list. This happens dozens of times a day.

RecommendationKeep filter state on back navigation and support opening records in a new tab.

4/5 affected
"That happens all the time... if I hit the back button, I don't have my list anymore. I have to search it again."P3 · training grants administrator, 20+ years

High severity

Search can't find awards the way people ask about them

PI name search didn't exist in the Awards tab. The PI filter required an exact "Last, First" format with no hint, and slow results had no loading state.

RecommendationAdd PI name search with flexible formats and a visible loading state.

5/5 affected
"The first time it did not give me anything, but then it finally did."P5 · School of Engineering

High severity

Finding one request means visiting a second system

Search accepted only internal application or request IDs, which grant managers rarely have when a PI calls. They looked the ID up in another portal, then came back to search again.

RecommendationAccept PI name and Award ID directly in SAGE search.

4/5 affected
"It's kind of time consuming to have to go back and forth between two different tabs."P2 · grants manager, Computer Science

Moderate severity

No export, so people copy data into spreadsheets by hand

This was the direct mechanism behind the shadow Excel system we set out to explain.

RecommendationCSV or Excel export that respects the current filters.

3/5 keep external sheets
"It would be great if I could download reports... without having to hunt it down and put it in a separate spreadsheet."P3

Stage 5 · Evaluation · Recommendations

Every fix assigned to the team that would build it

A list of problems handed to "the product team" tends to stall. We mapped each recommendation to an owning function so it could become a ticket the same week.

SeverityIssueRecommendationOwner
HighFilters lost on navigationPersist filter state; open in new tabEngineering, UX
HighLimited, inconsistent searchPI name search, flexible formats, loading statesProduct, Engineering
HighSearch needs an outside lookupAccept PI name and Award IDProduct, Engineering
ModerateNo data exportFilter-aware CSV / Excel exportEngineering, Product
ModerateList view lacks contextCustomizable columns: type, summary, next ownerDesign, Product
IrritantUnclear ownership"My requests" filter and ownership markersDesign, Engineering

Impact

"Excel is the real tool... BI Portal is an intermediate step."

From the product team's own synthesis, months later

The SAGE product team turned our recommendations into backlog tickets with priority levels. They accepted some, pushed back on others where business constraints differed from our priority calls, and flagged a few for more discovery.

Months later, while planning a larger migration, the team cross-analyzed three independent evaluations, including ours, and reached the same root diagnosis from their own data.

The pushback is part of the result. Research is an input to a decision, and watching a team weigh, accept and contest our findings showed me the study was taken seriously.

Reflection

What I'd keep, and what I'd change

Worked

  • Heuristic evaluation first kept scarce participant time focused.
  • Consistent error patterns across 4 of 5 people made the case hard to dismiss.
  • Owner-mapped recommendations moved straight into a backlog.

Limits

  • Only experienced users; novices haven't built workarounds yet.
  • N = 5 supports finding issues, not estimating how often they occur.
  • We didn't time tasks or log error rates systematically.

Next time

  • Add novice users as a comparison group.
  • Grow to 8 to 10 sessions and add time on task.
  • Include edge-case tasks where the system is most likely to break.

Should an AI show its answer before or after you decide?

QuantitativeCase study 02 · Online experiment

Who goes first matters: AI-first vs. human-first decisions

Every AI-assisted tool makes a design choice about when to show its recommendation. I ran a between-subjects experiment to see what that choice does to the mistakes people make.

My role
Lead researcher and first author: design, build, analysis, writing
Timeline
Sep 2025 to Aug 2026
Methods
Randomized experiment, interaction logs, confidence ratings, open-ended responses
Output
Full paper under review at CHI, with Yanheng Li and Sourojit Ghosh

The question

Should an AI show its recommendation first, or wait until the person commits to their own judgment? Most teams look only at overall accuracy.

What I did

A randomized study with 100 Prolific participants doing 24 AI-assisted X-ray screening decisions, with every click, zoom and AI toggle logged.

What I found

Same accuracy, different failures. AI-first users followed wrong AI flags 67% more often, while spending more time "verifying". The real choice is which error you can afford.

ContextStudy designHypothesesFindingsDesign guidanceReflection

Context

Accuracy dashboards hide how AI changes people's mistakes

Content moderation, clinical decision support and security screening all pair a person with an AI recommendation. Automation bias, over-relying on that recommendation, comes in two forms that have very different costs:

  • Commission errors: the AI raises a false alarm and the person follows it.
  • Omission errors: the AI misses a real problem and the person misses it too.

Prior work mostly reports whether a workflow raises or lowers overall accuracy. I wanted to know how workflow order changes the mix of errors and the behavior behind them, because that's what a product team actually needs to choose a design.

RQ1 · OutcomesHow does order affect accuracy, commission errors and omission errors?
RQ2 · BehaviorHow does order change how people verify and consult the AI?
RQ3 · CalibrationDoes knowing when you're right protect against bias in either workflow?

Stages 1–2 · Planning and research · Study design

Same images, same AI, only the order changes

I chose X-ray baggage screening because it is a standard paradigm in automation-bias research where right and wrong are unambiguous. That made it possible to plant exactly as many chances for each error type as I needed.

Design
2 workflow (between) × 2 AI correctness × 2 difficulty (within)
Participants
N = 100 on Prolific, randomized 50 / 50, desktop only, IRB approved
AI-first
Image and AI label shown together; users can hide the AI, then submit once
Human-first
Users submit an unaided call, then see the AI and may revise
Trials
24 per person: 12 AI-correct, 6 planted false alarms, 6 planted misses
Logged
Verification time, zoom / drag / draw use, AI toggles, AI-visible time, 0 to 100 confidence
Analysis
Welch's t-tests with Wilcoxon checks; mixed-effects logistic regression in R (lme4)
Calibration
Brier score from confidence vs. correctness, plus a non-overlapping-trials sensitivity check

Stage 1 · Planning · Hypotheses

What I expected, and what happened

I set four hypotheses from prior automation-bias research before collecting data. Three didn't hold, which is what made the result useful to a design team.

#HypothesisResultWhat the data showed
H1aAI-first causes more commission and omission errorsPartlyCommission only
H1bHuman-first gives higher accuracyNot supportedEqual overall, with a crossover by AI correctness
H2Human-first users verify moreNot supportedThe opposite: AI-first verified more
H3Calibration changes the workflow effectNot supportedBetter calibration helped in both workflows

Stage 3 · Synthesis · Findings

Order didn't change how often people were right. It changed how they were wrong.

1. Showing AI first trades one risk for another

When the AI was right, AI-first users were more accurate. When it was wrong, they were less accurate. Aggregate accuracy averaged these out to a tie, which is exactly why an accuracy-only dashboard would call the two designs equal.

"The AI tool made me unsure of my decisions... that made me more unsure even when I was pretty sure it was safe."AI-first participant

2. More verification did not mean more independent judgment

AI-first users spent 19.4 s verifying per trial vs. 10.5 s, and switched tools almost twice as often (2.8 vs. 1.5), yet made more commission errors. The AI label stayed on screen for 93% of their trial time vs. 10%. They were checking where the AI pointed. Effort metrics alone would have rated this the more careful workflow.

"I always zoomed on the area that the AI was suggesting, and then dragged around looking for things."AI-first participant

3. Deciding first helps, but the revision step leaks

In the human-first workflow, correct AI advice fixed 41% of wrong initial calls (75 of 181). Wrong AI advice also flipped 13% of correct calls (57 of 423), mostly when people felt unsure. Human-first used the AI as a second opinion, consulting it more often but briefly.

"If the answer was obvious, I did not even count what AI said. If I wasn't sure, I checked if my observation was the same as AI's."Human-first participant

4. Calibrated people resisted bias in both workflows

People whose confidence tracked their accuracy made fewer automation-bias errors under either design, with no evidence that calibration changed the workflow effect (interaction OR = 1.05, 95% CI 0.48 to 2.29). Calibration support is a lever that works alongside workflow choice.

"I felt uncertain when the AI's suggestion differed from my initial decision, which prompted me to re-examine the image."Human-first participant

Outcome · Design guidance

What I'd tell a team shipping an AI-assisted review tool

Choose the order by the cost of each error

If false alarms are expensive to act on, delay the AI. If the model is highly reliable and misses are the bigger risk, showing it first can help. Track commission and omission separately.

Use staged disclosure

Ask for a quick initial call, or reveal AI detail progressively, so people form a view before the recommendation frames what they look at.

Add friction where revisions go wrong

When someone is about to switch from their own answer to the AI's, highlight the disagreement or ask for a one-line reason.

Don't use time-on-task as a trust metric

Long inspection under constant AI exposure looked diligent and produced more bias. Measure where attention goes, not only how long it lasts.

Reflection

Two hypotheses failed, and that was the finding

Worked

  • Planting equal false alarms and misses let me separate the two error types cleanly.
  • Interaction logs explained the "why" that outcome data couldn't.
  • Open-ended responses gave the team quotable mechanisms.

Limits

  • Simulated AI and a lab task; real screeners have training and time pressure.
  • Crowd workers, not domain experts.
  • Open-ended responses illustrate patterns but weren't formally coded.

Next time

  • Pre-register hypotheses and a power analysis.
  • Test staged disclosure and revision friction as conditions.
  • Run with domain experts in a realistic tool.

Designing VR for anxious kids when parents and dentists also decide

GenerativeCase study 03 · Co-design

"Can I decorate my teeth with diamonds?"

Exploring how VR could ease children's dental anxiety, with the children designing it, and their parents and dentists telling us what would actually be allowed in the room.

My role
Lead researcher and first author: protocol, recruiting, facilitation, analysis
Timeline
Sep 2023 to Mar 2025
Methods
Co-design workshops, bodystorming, parent and dentist interviews, thematic analysis
Output
Published at ACM CSCW 2025 · BiWell Lab, CityU Hong Kong

The problem

Dental anxiety leads children to delay care. Sedation worries parents and therapy takes time. Existing VR tools mostly distract, and they're designed without the adults who decide whether a child uses them.

What I did

5 co-design workshops with 13 anxious children aged 10 to 12, parallel interviews with their 13 parents, and design reviews with 2 dentists.

What I found

Each group defined success differently. I turned the conflicts into six product requirements, including using different VR modes before and during treatment.

ContextMethodFindingsRequirementsReflection

Context

A product with three customers

A children's health product has a user who experiences it, a gatekeeper who decides whether the user gets it, and an operator who has to work around it. Designing only for the child produces something parents won't allow or dentists can't use mid-procedure. So the study put the child at the center and brought the adults in at the right moments.

RQ1 · VisionHow do children, parents and dentists imagine VR easing a child's dental anxiety?
RQ2 · ConstraintsWhat do parents and dentists need, and worry about, before they'd accept it?

Stage 2 · User research · Method

Letting 10-year-olds design, without the adults steering

Recruiting was the first hard problem. We screened 44 children with a standardized dental-fear scale (CFSS-DS) and kept 13 with moderate to severe anxiety. Strict criteria made online recruiting slow, so I printed posters and took them to elementary schools.

  1. Journey mapChildren mapped their last dental visit with comics: triggers, coping, what helped.
  2. VR inspiration5 minutes each in three Quest 2 apps: active play, a passive 360° film, a dental simulation.
  3. DesignSettings, characters and sounds with paper, Lego and plasticine, then bodystorming the interactions.
  4. PresentChildren demoed their designs and gave each other feedback.
  5. Adult reviewParents reacted to the designs; dentists reviewed summaries for safety and workflow.
Children
13, aged 10 to 12, in 5 workshops of 2 to 3, 150 to 210 min with long breaks
Parents
13, watched remotely from another room so they couldn't steer, then interviewed
Dentists
2 (one pediatric, one general), ~1 hour remote design reviews
Analysis
Reflexive thematic analysis; 3 coders, independent first pass, cross-checked

Stages 3–4 · Synthesis and modeling · Findings

One headset, three definitions of success

GroupThemeWhat it covers
ChildrenA · Prepare before treatmentExplore a virtual clinic, role-play the dentist, meet other scared kids
ChildrenB · Engage during treatmentControl while lying still, calm or cathartic play, hide stressors
ParentsC · Teach oral healthReplays after treatment, prevention built into everyday play
ParentsD · Protect health and contentEyesight, time limits, addiction, no violent content
DentistsE · Safety and workflowStillness, accurate previews, hospital purchasing and upkeep
DentistsF · Supplement, not substituteParents stay essential; one session isn't enough

Reading the six themes side by side gave a stakeholder map: the child as user, the parent as gatekeeper, the dentist as operator.

User

Children

Want
Control while lying still: a controller mounted on the chair. Friends who are scared too. A rehearsal where they play the dentist.
Surprise
Some wanted to blow off steam with combat games, not calm scenes.
"I hope it can support multiplayer mode so that I wouldn't feel lonely."C8

Gatekeeper

Parents

Want
VR that teaches oral hygiene, not just distraction, such as a replay of the procedure afterward.
Worry
Eyesight, screen time (about 30 minutes felt reasonable), addiction, and violent content.
Nearly all parents raised prolonged use and eyesight as their first concern.Pattern across parent interviews

Operator

Dentists

Want
A child who stays still. Calm, passive content during treatment and realistic previews beforehand.
Worry
Exciting games make kids move. VR could shift support away from parents. Hospitals must buy and maintain it.
"VR cannot replace any role."Dentist

The children's most exciting ideas were the ones dentists found most dangerous in the chair.

That tension shaped the main requirement: split the product by stage. Active, playful, social VR at home or in the waiting room before treatment. Calm, passive VR in the chair, where stillness matters.

Outcome · Product requirements

From conflicting needs to product requirements

Stage-based modes

Interactive before treatment, passive during. Resolves child excitement vs. dentist safety.

Adaptive exposure

Start cartoon-like, move toward realism as anxiety drops, and blur specific stressors. Resolves comfort vs. accurate expectations.

Control within limits

Chair-mounted input and open exploration that respects a still body.

Safe peer connection

Moderated shared spaces, with privacy designed in for minors.

Family co-selection

Parents and children choose content together, which turns parents' content limits into a shared ritual.

Clinical fit

Session time limits, no gore or aggression, staff training, equipment upkeep and consented record-keeping.

Reflection

What researching with children taught me

Worked

  • Hands-on materials and bodystorming got 10-year-olds past "make it fun".
  • Keeping parents in a separate room protected the children's ideas.
  • Dentist reviews grounded ideas in clinical reality early.

Limits

  • All participants in a Chinese context; 2 dentists only.
  • Concepts, not a working system, so no effectiveness data.
  • Families interested in technology were likelier to sign up.

Next time

  • Prototype the stage-based modes and test them in a clinic.
  • Recruit more dentists and dental nurses.
  • Follow families over multiple visits.

Aura Focus: a task manager for adults with ADHD

End to endCase study 04 · Mixed methods

Getting started shouldn't be the hardest part

Aura Focus is a task manager for adults with ADHD. We took it through all five research stages in a five-day research sprint, from a survey to paper-prototype tests.

My role
UX researcher and product manager, team of 4 with Manasvi Kale, Sara Choi, Kohji Andriani
Timeline
Fall 2025 · 5 days of research
Methods
Survey, interviews, secondary research, affinity mapping, personas, paper prototyping, utility testing
Context
UW HCDE 518, User-Centered Design

The problem

Most productivity tools assume rigid schedules, steady focus and manual sorting, which are the executive functions people with ADHD find hardest to sustain.

What we did

A survey of 35 adults with ADHD, interviews, and secondary research, synthesized in an affinity map and three personas, then paper-prototype and utility tests.

What changed

Six design changes, each traced to a participant. The biggest: suggestions people can override, with the reason shown.

1 · Planning2 · Research3 · Synthesis4 · Modeling5 · EvaluationReflection

Stage 1 · Planning

How might we help adults with ADHD manage daily tasks and feel more capable and connected?

ChallengesWhat task-management problems do adults with ADHD face every day?
Current behaviorHow do they organize, prioritize and finish tasks, and what motivates or discourages them?
Adaptive designHow can a tool personalize support without adding cognitive load or taking away control?

With five days for research, I planned each method to answer a different kind of question: the survey for patterns, interviews for motivations, secondary research to frame the problem.

Stage 2 · User research

Existing tools didn't fit how people with ADHD work

Survey
35 adults with ADHD: organization strategies, emotional responses, tool use
Interviews
Semi-structured, on motivation, task initiation and coping
Prioritizing
53% said it is the hardest part of organizing their day
Current tools
Over 55% found them unhelpful
One participant wished the tool could tell them in advance how long each task takes, because time blindness makes them underestimate everything.P2, paraphrased

Stage 3 · Synthesis

An affinity map, down to four insights

Autonomy starts tasks

People wanted to decide in the moment. "I'd rather... decide in the moment."

Rigidity drains

Strict structure created emotional fatigue and stalled follow-through.

Time is invisible

Time blindness made people underestimate every task.

Tools miss specific needs

Over half found current tools unhelpful because they assume one way of working.

Stage 4 · UX modeling

Three kinds of task managers

We used the personas to align the team on who we were designing for. They were not treated as validation: design decisions still came from what participants said in testing.

Stage 5 · Evaluation

Paper prototypes first, then a utility test

The utility test covered five questions: gamification and social motivation, energy and cognitive load, autonomy and manual control, positive feedback loops, and how much guidance to give.

What we heard (paraphrased)What we changedWho
Wants to know how long tasks takeEstimate duration and energy level from past tasksP2
Gets sidetracked by tasks in other roomsSpatial anchors show only the current room's tasksP5
Wants to see the logic and adjust itManual override slot, with the reason for each suggestionP4
Likes categories already set upVoice input that auto-tags time, place and energyP2
Don't highlight failure at day's endUnfinished tasks roll over neutrally as "pending"UT
Prefers social rewards to the puzzleSmall, opt-in friends leaderboardUT

Reflection

A full cycle on a tight clock

Worked

  • Mixed methods gave breadth and depth in five days.
  • The iteration table kept design honest to evidence.
  • Override control came straight from participants.

Limits

  • A short sprint and a small interview sample.
  • Personas are synthesized, not validated.
  • Paper prototypes can't test the AR experience itself.

Next time

  • Diary study to see real task-starting moments.
  • Test an interactive prototype over several days.
  • Measure task initiation, not just preference.
